nameStory: Nordmann's Orbweaver is named after Alexander von Nordmann, a 19th-century Finnish-Russian naturalist who explored and catalogued wildlife across Europe and Asia. This spider's name reflects its wide distribution across northern regions, from North America all the way to Japan, following some of the same territories Nordmann once studied.
description: Nordmann's Orbweaver is a medium-sized spider that builds classic circular webs with radiating spokes and spiral threads. Like other orbweavers, it has a rounded, somewhat flattened abdomen and relatively short legs compared to web-hunters like wolf spiders. These spiders typically measure about the size of a dime including their legs, with females being noticeably larger than males. They're part of the diverse Araneus genus, which includes many of New England's most recognizable garden spiders.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds the classic orb web - a flat, circular design with radiating spokes and a spiral of sticky capture thread. The web feels substantial and slightly elastic when gently touched with a grass blade.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, slightly flattened abdomen that's wider than it is tall, giving it a somewhat humped appearance when viewed from the side. The body feels firm but not hard if gently examined.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length typically ranges from small to medium for orbweavers, with females noticeably larger than the smaller, more slender males. Total size including legs spans roughly the diameter of a quarter.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web or retreats to nearby vegetation, connected by a signal thread that vibrates when prey is caught. Active primarily at night when web maintenance occurs.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two rows, though they're quite small and difficult to see clearly without magnification. The eyes appear as tiny dark dots on the front of the head region.

habitat: Found in a variety of habitats including gardens, forest edges, meadows, and areas with mixed vegetation where they can anchor their webs between plants. They prefer spots with some shelter nearby - bushes, tall grasses, or structures where they can retreat from their web when not actively hunting. Like many orbweavers, they're adaptable to both wild and human-modified landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders begin appearing and establishing small webs as they grow. Look for smaller webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season with full-sized webs most visible. Adults are actively hunting and mating during warm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Mated females produce egg sacs before the first frost. Webs may become more noticeable as morning dew makes them sparkle in autumn light.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die with the first hard frost. Eggs overwinter in protected silk sacs, often hidden under bark or in plant debris.

funFact: This spider is one of nature's true world travelers - the exact same species spins webs in New England backyards, Korean forests, Russian steppes, and Japanese gardens, making it one of the most geographically widespread orbweavers on Earth.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other medium-sized Araneus orbweavers like the Cross Orbweaver or Marbled Orbweaver. The key is focusing on the overall web structure and behavior rather than trying to distinguish subtle body markings, which can vary significantly even within the same species. When in doubt, note the habitat and web location for better identification context.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Araneus simply means 'spider' in Latin and includes many of the orbweavers people think of as typical 'garden spiders.' Despite sharing the Araneus genus with famous species like Charlotte from Charlotte's Web (the Barn Orbweaver), Nordmann's Orbweaver is less well-known but equally skilled at web construction.
compareHints: Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance). It tends to be more subtle in coloration and pattern, making it one of the 'plain Jane' members of this diverse genus. The web structure and building behavior are nearly identical across Araneus species, so habitat preferences and geographic range often provide better identification clues than appearance alone.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
